q: Why are index fossils most useful when they evolved rapidly?
choices: They occur through a short time interval, so they narrow the age of a rock layer
They are always the largest fossils
They can only live in deep oceans
They make absolute radiometric dates
explanation: Rapid evolution means a species exists for a relatively short geologic interval. If that fossil is found in a rock, it narrows the time window in which the rock was deposited.

q: William Smith is especially important to historical geology because he…
choices: Discovered radioactive decay
Recognized fossil succession and produced an early geologic map
Proposed mantle convection
Discovered sea-floor spreading
explanation: Smith noticed that fossil assemblages occur in a predictable order and used them to correlate strata. That insight helped him construct an early geologic map.

q: Why can the same index fossil correlate rock layers far apart?
choices: It must have a wide geographic distribution
It must be restricted to one tiny habitat
It must live for hundreds of millions of years
It must occur only in igneous rocks
explanation: A useful index fossil is geographically widespread, so the same species can appear in distant outcrops. Its short time range then links those layers to roughly the same interval.

q: Which statement best describes catastrophism in the historical-geology debate?
choices: Earth changes only at today's rates
Major geologic changes and extinctions can occur during catastrophic events
All rocks crystallized from magma
Fossils cannot be used for correlation
explanation: Catastrophism emphasized abrupt, large-scale events and discontinuities in the rock record. Bretz later showed that catastrophic flooding could be a real geologic process.

All continents move because of mantle convection
Earth formed from one giant impact
Mountains are only built by erosion
explanation: Neptunism treated a universal ocean as the major source from which rocks formed. It was an attempt to explain local rock observations with a global cause.

q: Plutonism/Vulcanism emphasized which source of rocks and geologic change?
choices: Only biological activity
Molten material and Earth's internal heat
A universal ocean only
Meteor impacts only
explanation: Plutonism emphasized igneous processes—molten rock solidifying—and internal heat as a major driver of Earth change.

q: What is the key difference between actualism and gradualism?
choices: Actualism says natural laws/processes are comparable through time; gradualism says rates/intensities are also similar
They are exactly the same idea
Actualism is about fossils; gradualism is about minerals
Actualism requires catastrophes while gradualism forbids erosion
explanation: Actualism is the safer principle: the same natural laws and processes operate through time. Gradualism adds a stronger claim that rates and intensities are similar, which is not always true.

q: What did Hutton emphasize about Earth?
choices: It was static and unchanged
It was an evolving system driven partly by internal heat
It formed only a few thousand years ago
All rocks came from a global flood
explanation: Hutton saw Earth as dynamic and continually changing, with internal heat playing an important role in uplift, melting, and recycling.

q: Why was strict Lyell-style gradualism eventually too restrictive?
choices: Because rare high-intensity events can also shape Earth
Because erosion was proven impossible
Because fossils stopped being useful
Because natural laws changed through time
explanation: The same processes can operate through time without always operating at the same rate or intensity. Giant floods, impacts, eruptions, and other rare events can matter enormously.

q: What made Bretz's Channeled Scablands interpretation controversial?
choices: He proposed enormous floods when many geologists strongly favored gradual explanations
He denied that water could erode rock
He claimed the Scablands were volcanic
He used radiometric dating before it existed
explanation: Bretz argued that landforms in the Scablands required huge, short-lived floods. That clashed with the strong preference at the time for slow, gradual change.

q: What did J.T. Pardee's work contribute to the Scablands story?
choices: Evidence supporting the giant-flood interpretation
Proof that no flood occurred
The first fossil map of England
The discovery of plate tectonics
explanation: Pardee's evidence helped support the idea that catastrophic outburst floods actually occurred, strengthening Bretz's interpretation.

q: The professor's scientific-method question ‘How will I know if I'm wrong?’ is mainly asking whether a hypothesis…
choices: Makes testable predictions that could fail
Sounds convincing
Matches the textbook wording
Has no alternative explanations
explanation: A useful scientific hypothesis must be testable. You should be able to identify observations or experiments that would contradict its predictions.
